title: Chanting for the Sick
hookLine: an old hymn sends a cough flying, and families still chant a Rig Veda verse at the bedside
carry: hindus chant for the sick, alongside the medicine
tomorrow: why do so many Hindu homes water one plant every morning?
last: THE SACRED IS IN YOUR HANDS.

lines: A LECTURE, A BARGAIN, OR DIRECTIONS?
cards: Some ailments get a lecture. Some get a bargain. In one short Atharva Veda hymn, a cough gets something stranger: directions.
Three verses, and in each one the speaker points the cough toward the horizon and tells it to go. Not to die, just to leave, fast and far.
Anyone propped up on pillows at night, tired of the rattle in their chest, knows the wish. Here it's poetry, all speed and distance.

teach.h: AS THE MIND FLIES, FLY OFF.
teach.b: Here is the hymn, in paraphrase. As the mind, with its wishes, flies swiftly far away, so, cough, fly off along the mind's own course. As a sharpened arrow flies swiftly far, so, cough, fly off across the wide earth.
As the rays of the sun fly swiftly far, so, cough, fly off along the surge of the sea. The cough is kasa, and the hymn speaks straight to it, as if words could reach it.

teach.h: A MANTRA IS AN ACT, NOT JUST A SOUND.
teach.b: That's the Vedic faith in speech: a mantra said with care is an act, not just a sound. And it's why Hindu families still chant for the sick.
The verse many turn to comes from the Rig Veda: the Mahamrityunjaya, the great death-conquering mantra. Families tie it to the story of Markandeya, a boy fated to die at sixteen.
When Yama, lord of death, threw his noose, the boy held tight to a Shiva linga, and Shiva burst out of it and drove death back.
Om tryambakam yajamahe. In paraphrase: we worship the three-eyed one, Shiva, fragrant, who makes life grow. As a ripe cucumber slips from its vine, may I be freed from death, not from the deathless.
Families chant it a hundred and eight times on a mala, play it softly by a hospital bed, or gather on a call to say it together.
Many teachers read what it asks this way: not never to die, to be let go gently, like ripe fruit, toward what doesn't die.
And to be plain: this is prayer, not treatment. Hindus chant beside the doctor's care, never instead of it, and a cough that hangs on belongs with a doctor.

how: Vedic hymns for the sick are kept in recitation from teacher to student; many Hindu families chant the Mahamrityunjaya mantra, often 108 times on a mala, for someone who is ill, alongside medical care.

o: a prayer said for her, alongside the doctors' care

games.why: in the Vedic view words act: a mantra said with care is an offering. Hindus chant for the sick beside the medicine, not instead of it.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell. If you pray, say the mantra's opening slowly, om tryambakam yajamahe, or simply their name, three times, the way many Hindus pray for the sick.
If you don't, hold that person in mind for three slow breaths and wish them well. Then pick one plain thing to do for them today: a text, a meal, a call.

sources.ref: Atharva Veda 6.105.1–3 (as the mind, as a sharpened arrow, as the sun's rays fly swiftly far, so, cough, fly off along the mind's course, the earth's expanse, the sea's surge)
Rig Veda 7.59.12 (we worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, who increases nourishment; like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be freed from death, not from immortality)
Markandeya and Shiva as Kalantaka, ender of death (Puranic story, told in several Puranas and at temples such as Thirukkadaiyur; its link to this mantra is popular tradition)
